source.author: verg
source.text: Nec mora: continuo vastis cum viribus effert ora Dares, magnoque virum se murmure tollit; solus qui Paridem solitus contendere contra, idemque ad tumulum, quo maximus occubat Hector, victorem Buten immani corpore, qui se Bebrycia veniens Amyci de gente ferebat, perculit, et fulva moribundum extendit harena.
source.text_original: Nec mora: continuo vastis cum viribus effert / ora Dares, magnoque virum se murmure tollit; / solus qui Paridem solitus contendere contra, / idemque ad tumulum, quo maximus occubat Hector, / victorem Buten immani corpore, qui se / Bebrycia veniens Amyci de gente ferebat, / perculit, et fulva moribundum extendit harena.
source.text_english: Without delay: at once Dares lifts his face with mighty strength and raises himself amid a great murmur of the men; he, the one who alone was accustomed to contend against Paris, and likewise, by the mound where great Hector lies dead, struck down the victorious Butes with his enormous body, he who, coming from Bebrycia and boasting himself to be of the race of Amycus, and stretched him dying on the golden sand.

reuse.author: hier
reuse.text: nos nostra habuimus tempora et cucurrimus, quantum potuimus; nunc te currente et longa spatia transmittente nobis debetur otium simulque, ut cum uenia et honore tuo dixerim, ne solus mihi de poetis aliquid proposuisse uidearis, memento Daretis et Entelli et uulgaris prouerbii, quod bos lassus fortius figat pedem.
reuse.text_original: nos nostra habuimus tempora et cucurrimus, quantum potuimus; nunc te currente et longa spatia transmittente nobis debetur otium simulque, ut cum uenia et honore tuo dixerim, ne solus mihi de poetis aliquid proposuisse uidearis, memento Daretis et Entelli et uulgaris prouerbii, quod bos lassus fortius figat pedem.
reuse.text_english: We have had our times, and we have run as far as we could; now, since you are running and covering long stretches for us, leisure is owed to us, and at the same time, if I may say so with your pardon and honor, so that you may not seem to me to have proposed only something about the poets, remember Dares and Entellus and the common proverb that a tired ox sets its foot more firmly.
